extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film enthusiasts, and aspiring film critics interested in Roger Ebert's life and critical approach
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria drawn from Roger Ebert's biography about how he judged films and wrote reviews: accessible, emotionally honest, stylistically focused criticism that champions underseen work and communicates to non-specialists. Useful for someone modeling or evaluating film reviews in Ebert's tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertaining, direct, accessible prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing in a prose style intended to be entertaining and direct; making sophisticated cinematic and analytical ideas more accessible to non-specialist audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert wrote to be entertaining and direct so that complex cinematic ideas become understandable to mainstream readers. Use clear, lively language rather than academic jargon; aim to inform and engage non-specialist audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional honesty as a guide
rubrics_metrics.description: “Your intellect may be confused, but your emotions never lie to you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and acknowledge your emotional response to a film — treat genuine emotional reaction as a truthful input into criticism, even when analysis is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a movie on its style (how it conveys its subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It's not what a movie is about, it's how it's about what it's about.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the film's manner of expression — mise-en-scène, pacing, tone, technique — rather than only summarizing or debating plot/subject matter. Focus analysis on execution and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open to the immediate experience; set aside theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should 'set aside theory and ideology, theology and politics, and open himself to—well, the immediate experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach screenings by attending to what happens to you in the theater first, rather than filtering the film through preformed theoretical/ideological frameworks. Let the viewing experience drive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star-rating system is relative and contextual
rubrics_metrics.description: He awarded four stars to films of the highest quality, and generally a half star to those of the lowest, unless he considered the film to be 'artistically inept and morally repugnant', in which case it received no stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use star/score systems as shorthand within the context of the review: ratings are comparative (e.g., 'if Superman is four, then Hellboy is three'). Explain the scale and contextualize the rating with the review text; reserve 'no stars' for films judged artistically inept and morally repugnant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-spoken, genial, conversational presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert's prose had a 'plain-spoken Midwestern clarity...a genial, conversational presence on the page' and 'rarely seems to be showing off.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a modest, conversational tone that avoids literary showiness. Aim for clarity and approachability; avoid ostentation that distances the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dry wit and deadpan humor to highlight flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert's reviews were characterized by 'dry wit.' He often wrote in a deadpan style when discussing a movie's flaws (example: his multi-paragraph takedown of Jaws: The Revenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ understated, witty phrasing and deadpan comparisons to make criticisms memorable and entertaining. Use humor to underscore points without merely mocking for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include personal anecdotes to connect and illustrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert often included personal anecdotes in his reviews to anchor responses (example: memories of Saturday matinees when reviewing The Last Picture Show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise personal recollections to situate your reaction, illustrate a point, or explain why a film affected you. Personal detail should illuminate rather than distract from analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with form when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: He sometimes wrote reviews in the forms of stories, poems, songs, scripts, open letters, or imagined conversations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to nonstandard review forms when they serve insight or rhetorical effect. Formal experimentation can illuminate a film's qualities or make a review more engaging, but should still clarify judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Champion foreign, independent, and underseen films for mainstream audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert endorsed foreign and independent films he believed would be appreciated by mainstream viewers, championing filmmakers like Werner Herzog, Errol Morris and Spike Lee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recommend worthwhile underseen films and explain why mainstream audiences should care. Bridge gaps of familiarity by describing accessibility and appeal rather than assuming specialist knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take animation and documentary seriously as cinema
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert championed animation (e.g., Hayao Miyazaki, Isao Takahata) and documentaries (e.g., Errol Morris's Gates of Heaven), arguing they can offer unique cinematic experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess animation and documentary on their own artistic terms; argue for their aesthetic possibilities and cultural importance rather than treating them as lesser categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend aesthetic/technical choices (e.g., black-and-white) with argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert argued for the aesthetic values of black-and-white photography and against colorization, describing black-and-white as 'more dreamlike, more pure' and a legitimate artistic choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating technical or aesthetic choices, explain their expressive effects (e.g., mood, composition) rather than dismissing them. Articulate why a choice succeeds or fails for that film's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve scathing, memorable condemnation for truly egregious films
rubrics_metrics.description: Although he rarely wrote outright scathing reviews, when he hated a film he wrote memorable, forceful condemnations (examples: North: 'I hated this movie. Hated hated hated...' ; Mad Dog Time: 'the first movie I have seen that does not improve on the sight of a blank screen...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, emphatic language sparingly and with concrete justification — make strong condemnations specific and rhetorically effective rather than gratuitous.
